== APPRAISAL INSTRUCTIONS (GEMINI_HANDOFF_BRIEF §3 Task D; RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2; APPRAISAL_FORM.md; CODEBOOK.md §8) ==
1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:
   - If `Retrieval status` is `not_accessible` (or the paper text below says `[FULL TEXT NOT ACCESSIBLE]`), you MUST set `paper_read = "not accessible"`, `study_design_identified = "cannot_tell (full text not accessible)"`, `chosen_tool = "cannot_tell"`, `why_tool_chosen = "full text not accessible"`, `overall_rating = "cannot_tell"`, `domain_ratings = []`, all 7 `cross_tool_domains` fields to `"cannot_tell"`, `overall_narrative_summary = "Full text not accessible; no risk-of-bias appraisal performed."`, `where_found_summary = "not accessible"`, and `evidence_quotes = []`. NEVER guess study design or bias ratings from citation/title!

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Can't tell / No information — Cross-sectional qualitative case study drawing on earlier doctoral fieldwork (Kachenje, 2017); participant refusals, non-response, and incomplete interviews or focus groups are not reported.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern (not formally applicable to qualitative thematic description, but unaddressed in cross-scheme comparisons) — When comparing administrative responsiveness across the public (30 days), private (3 days), and community-based (6 days) schemes (Table 1, PDF p. 12), differences in scheme scale, customer volume, network complexity, and neighbourhood socioeconomic context are not accounted for.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate-to-weak — Key Tanzanian statutes and policies are identified by title and year (Local Government [Urban Authorities] Act No. 7 of 1982, EWURA Act 2001, National Water Policy 2002, NWSDS 2006, Water Resources Management Act No. 11 of 2009, and Water Supply and Sanitation Act 2019; PDF pp. 2, 9-10, 12), and de jure vs. de facto mandate frictions (e.g., DAWASA vs. municipal councils, Wami-Ruvu Basin Water Office abstraction permits vs. service licensing) are coherently mapped. However, specific statutory sections are not cited, Figure 1 (the institutional framework diagram on PDF p. 10) is blank in the published PDF, and empirical fieldwork from 2017 is blended with post-2019 statutory changes without clear temporal separation.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern — Although four data collection methods (document analysis, key informant interviews, focus group discussions, and household interviews) are stated (PDF pp. 1, 2, 7), no interview/FGD guides, recording procedures, field dates, or operationalized coding definitions are reported, and empirical findings rely heavily on unattributed assertions rather than verifiable primary data.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak — Water service delivery outcomes are barely measured empirically; the sole concrete service metric is maximum waiting time for new connection processing across the three schemes (30, 3, and 6 days in Table 1, PDF p. 12, cited to Kachenje 2017 without sample size, distribution, or audit source), while household water access, reliability, quality, and tariff affordability are not systematically measured.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: High concern — Substantial selective/incomplete reporting: the Data Analysis section claims that photographs, boxes, summaries, tables, figures, and direct quotations were used to present data from interviews, FGDs, and household interviews (PDF pp. 7-8), yet the published paper contains zero household or FGD data, zero photographs or boxes, only one brief quote from a utility official (PDF p. 14), and a blank Figure 1 diagram on PDF p. 10.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern — Three water supply schemes (one public, one private, one community-based) in Dar es Salaam were purposively selected using unstated selection criteria (PDF p. 7; schemes and neighbourhoods are never named), sample sizes and recruitment methods for key informants, focus groups, and households are completely omitted, and water vending was deliberately excluded despite its acknowledged importance for underserved urban residents (PDF pp. 1, 15).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was there a clear statement of the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper clearly states its aim to analyze institutional coordination processes and factors hindering effective multi-actor coordination in urban municipal water supply delivery in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, and to recommend ways to overcome these challenges (though the specific research questions mentioned in Methods are not listed verbatim).

domain_ratings.justification: A qualitative methodology grounded in coordination, institutional, and social network theories is well suited to exploring inter-organizational relationships, formal and informal rules, actor mandates, and stakeholder mindsets across public, private, and community-based water delivery systems.
domain_ratings.where_found: Introduction (PDF pp. 2-3); Methods — Materials and Methods (PDF p. 7)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the research design appropriate to address the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The author justifies a comparative multiple-case study design examining three distinct water supply schemes (public, private, and community-based) as units of analysis in Dar es Salaam in order to capture how actor roles and coordination mechanisms operate across differing service-delivery governance models.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods — Materials and Methods, Research Design and Process, and Sample design and the smallest unit of analysis (PDF pp. 7-8)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the recruitment strategy appropriate to the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: Although the paper states that three schemes were selected using 'specific selection criteria' to minimize subjectivity, those criteria are never stated (the sentence on PDF p. 7 ends abruptly), the three chosen localities/schemes in Dar es Salaam are never identified, and there is zero information on how many key informants, households, or focus group participants were recruited or how they were selected. Water vending actors were also excluded a priori.
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Methods — Materials and Methods & Sample design (PDF pp. 7-8); Conclusions (PDF p. 15)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data collected in a way that addressed the research issue?
domain_ratings.justification: While four appropriate instruments are named (document analysis, key informant interviews, focus group discussions, and household interviews), the paper provides no details on interview/FGD topic guides, number of interviews/FGDs/households conducted, fieldwork dates (empirical data appear to stem from the author's 2017 thesis), audio recording vs. note-taking, interview settings, or data saturation. Moreover, Figure 1 on PDF p. 10 is blank in the published article.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Has the relationship between researcher and participants been adequately considered?
domain_ratings.justification: There is no discussion of researcher reflexivity, positionality, or potential researcher influence during scheme selection, interview question formulation, data collection, or interpretation.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods (PDF pp. 7-8 — absence of reflexivity discussion)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Have ethical issues been taken into consideration?
domain_ratings.justification: A one-sentence note at the end of the article states that institutional permission letters were sent and respondent consent was sought, but there is no mention of formal research ethics committee/IRB review, how informed consent was explained or documented, or how participant confidentiality and anonymity were protected when discussing inter-institutional conflicts.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data analysis sufficiently rigorous?
domain_ratings.justification: Although the author describes using quick impression/contact summaries and variable-guided thematic sorting across the three scheme categories, rigorous analytic transparency is lacking: coding frameworks are not shown, contradictory data are not examined, and virtually no primary empirical evidence is presented to substantiate thematic claims—there are zero focus group or household interview excerpts, zero boxes or photographs (despite claiming their use on PDF p. 8), and only a single short quote from one public utility respondent in the entire Results section.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods — Data analysis (PDF p. 8); Results and Discussion (PDF pp. 8-14)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there a clear statement of findings?
domain_ratings.justification: The five overarching coordination challenges (multiplicity of competing institutions, poor enforcement of regulatory instruments, bureaucratic delays in connection processing, lack of inter-model coordination mechanisms, and adversarial/dismissive mindsets among actors) are clearly organized and explicitly stated in relation to the research aim, even though primary evidentiary backing and discussion of counter-arguments are thin.
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Results and Discussion (PDF pp. 8-14); Conclusions (PDF pp. 14-15)

domain_ratings.justification: Narrative assessment: The paper offers useful institutional context on statutory versus practical governance frictions in Dar es Salaam's decentralized urban water sector—particularly vertical centralization within DAWASA, overlapping permitting by the Wami-Ruvu Basin Water Office, revenue-sharing tensions with Mtaa committees, and non-recognition of informal borehole operators—and outlines sensible policy and research questions. However, its empirical contribution and transferability are substantially limited by unreported sample sizes and site details, unpresented household/FGD data, exclusion of water vending, and reliance on earlier 2017 thesis material without systematic empirical updating.
domain_ratings.where_found: Results and Discussion (PDF pp. 9-14); Conclusions (PDF pp. 14-15)

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: S525 (Kachenje, 2025) is a primary qualitative comparative case study examining institutional coordination challenges across public, private, and community-based urban water supply schemes in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, drawing on coordination, institutional, and network theories. Appraised with the CASP Qualitative Checklist, the study raises high methodological concern (4 'Yes', 2 'No', and 3 'Can't tell' ratings across Q1-Q9, plus constrained empirical value on Q10). While the research aim (Q1), qualitative approach (Q2), comparative three-scheme case design (Q3), and thematic summary of five coordination barriers (Q9) are clearly articulated, fundamental reporting and evidentiary omissions undermine internal credibility. Specifically, the three studied schemes/neighbourhoods are never named, the 'specific selection criteria' mentioned on PDF p. 7 are omitted, and sample sizes and recruitment procedures for key informant interviews, focus group discussions, and household interviews are wholly unreported (Q4, Q5). Researcher reflexivity is absent (Q6), ethical reporting is limited to a single sentence noting institutional permission letters and participant consent without ethics board details (Q7), and analytic rigor/reporting is weak (Q8): despite claiming household interviews, focus groups, photographs, boxes, and direct quotations (PDF pp. 7-8), the Results section presents only one brief utility official quote (PDF p. 14), one descriptive summary table drawn from the author's 2017 doctoral thesis (Table 1, PDF p. 12), and a blank institutional diagram (Figure 1, PDF p. 10), while excluding water vending entirely.
raw_response.overall_rating: High methodological concern (2 No and 3 Can't tell items)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Qualitative comparative multiple-case study (examining one public, one private, and one community-based water supply scheme in Dar es Salaam using document analysis, key informant interviews, focus group discussions, and household interviews)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Introduction (PDF pp. 2-3); Methods — Materials and Methods, Research Design and Process, Sample design, and Data analysis (PDF pp. 7-8); Results and Discussion including Figure 1 and Table 1 (PDF pp. 8-14); Conclusions (PDF pp. 14-15); Ethical considerations and Data availability (PDF p. 17).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The Methods section explicitly characterizes the research as a qualitative multiple-case study ('The study was largely qualitative, and deployed a case study methodology', PDF p. 7; 'basically qualitative on the study phenomenon', PDF p. 8) using document analysis, key informant interviews, focus group discussions, and household interviews analyzed via contact summaries and thematic/content analysis. Although Table 1 (PDF p. 12, sourced from Kachenje 2017) reports illustrative maximum connection-processing days (30, 3, 6) and actor counts (5, 2, 3) for the three cases, there is no quantitative survey component or statistical analysis, making the CASP Qualitative Checklist (rather than MMAT or JBI Cross-Sectional) the exact matching appraisal tool.
